articles.title: Russian drone strike kills 14 at Ukraine train station as Moscow reports massive drone attack
articles.body:
KIEV/MOSCOW, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- At least 14 people were killed and 14 others injured Thursday when a Russian drone struck a railway station in Dnipro, central Ukraine, local authorities said.
Six of the injured, including an 11-year-old boy, were in serious condition, according to the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration.
Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said a jet-powered drone hit a platform where a train bound for Zaporizhzhia was stationary. Emergency services were working at the scene.
Separately, Russia's Defense Ministry said Thursday that its air defenses had intercepted 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight across multiple Russian regions.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said 613 drones had headed toward the Moscow region overnight, with 231 shot down as they approached the capital.
Russian media described the assault as one of the largest drone attacks on the country in the past year.
The Russian Defense Ministry also said its forces had struck a dry cargo ship bound for the port of Odesa, claiming it was carrying military and dual-use supplies for Ukrainian forces. ■

articles.title: Under Sanctions, Russia Turns to Africa With Plans to Relocate Industrial Production
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Under Sanctions, Russia Turns to Africa With Plans to Relocate Industrial Production
Russia is ready to move part of its industrial enterprises to Africa, Russian leader Vladimir Putin announced on October 29, The Moscow Times reported the same day.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"This fully corresponds to Russia's interests, especially today, when numerous sanctions are being applied to the Russian economy and Russian enterprises," Putin stated at the Russia-Africa forum. He described the investment potential of Russian companies as "fairly high" and added that "there is work to be done here."
Putin stressed that investments in African countries must be "reliable and protected." Plants would then operate "regardless of the foreign policy situation," he explained.
He was responding to Burundian President Évariste Ndayishimiye, who argued that Africa must go beyond exporting raw materials and importing finished goods.
"We must develop our own industrial potential, modernize our agriculture, strengthen our energy infrastructure and logistics routes, and invest more in research and technology development," Ndayishimiye told the forum. He emphasized that Africa should become "a real market for production and sales" rather than remain a consumer market.
A day earlier, Putin told 22 African leaders, including those of Ethiopia, Zimbabwe and Mali, that Russia had achieved "impressive results" in high technology. He said Moscow was ready to share its know-how with its "African friends." Competitors "have to catch up with us in some areas and copy our developments," he emphasized.
Russian ministers and state companies have since set out their own offers. Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov announced that Russian companies were ready to manufacture goods in African countries under industrial cooperation.
"The main message we bring to Africa is: let's ensure sovereign development together," he stated. Reshetnikov proposed cooperation in pharmaceuticals and IT solutions. Industry and Trade Minister Anton Alikhanov expressed readiness to develop automobile manufacturing in partnership with African partners.
Rosatom proposed building floating nuclear power plants in coastal African countries. "As a starting step, a source such as a floating nuclear power unit could be a good entry point to both solve their tasks and join the nuclear club," a representative of the state corporation explained.
Russia's largest liquefied natural gas producer, Novatek, offered African countries its own production technology, proven on Arctic projects. Aluminum giant Rusal signed a memorandum with Ghana on a joint venture to mine and process bauxite, the raw material for aluminum.
Moscow's push into African markets follows steep losses in its traditional energy trade since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Gazprom has lost more than half of its exports outside the former Soviet Union, with Russian gas exports expected to total about 77 billion cubic meters in 2026, down from 185 billion in 2021.
Exports are projected to fall to 72 billion cubic meters by 2028 once the EU gas embargo takes effect, a level last seen in the second half of the 1980s. Efforts to offset the losses through a major new supply deal with China have stalled over pricing, leaving talks on the proposed Power of Siberia 2 pipeline suspended.

articles.title: Houthi media claims 12 killed in airstrikes on residential houses in Yemen's Taiz
articles.body:
SANAA, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- At least 12 people were killed and three others critically wounded on Thursday in airstrikes on two residential houses in Yemen's southwestern province of Taiz, the Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported.
The outlet claimed the strikes hit homes in the Al-Barh area of Maqbanah district in western Taiz, blaming what it described as "Saudi aggression" for the attack, without providing further details.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia or Yemen's internationally recognized government on the reported strikes and casualties.
The reported airstrikes came as fighting intensified across Taiz, where Houthi forces and government forces have been battling on multiple fronts for control of the strategically important province.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said on Monday that severe access restrictions in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, have pushed health needs to critical levels amid shortages of medicine, fuel and water.
OCHA said continued fighting has also led to a buildup of uncollected waste, increasing the risk of disease outbreaks.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the north, prompting the Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the government. ■

articles.title: Interview: China is a key contributor to COP17 negotiations, says conference president
articles.body:
YEREVAN, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China has made significant contributions to advancing negotiations at the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), from pre-conference dialogue in Kunming to the ongoing global review of collective progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF), COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan told Xinhua.
Matevosyan said China has played a key role in the negotiations on and implementation of the KMGBF.
China chaired COP15, which was hosted by Canada, and facilitated the adoption of the KMGBF, one of the landmark global environmental agreements. Drawing on their experience, Chinese and Canadian colleagues can support the presidency in advancing progress on the global review, he said.
Matevosyan noted that the core task of COP17 is to complete the first global review of progress under the KMGBF and deliver on the Yerevan Pathway, shifting global efforts from pledges to tangible action to conserve nature.
"A majority of parties have submitted their national reports, laying an objective foundation for the assessment. Available evidence shows the world is far from reaching the 2030 targets," he said, noting that the first-ever global review of collective progress towards the KMGBF in Yerevan is of critical importance because it will clarify how close the world is to achieving its goals and identify implementation gaps.
Beyond the negotiations, China took the lead in establishing the Kunming Biodiversity Fund in 2021, contributing its own resources to help developing countries strengthen their conservation capacity. Officially launched in 2024, the fund offers new opportunities and helps turn decisions made at COP meetings into tangible results, he said.
Matevosyan said China and Armenia are already cooperating on national parks and protected areas.
"I had the honor of visiting China's Botanical Garden and China's Elephant Park during the Kunming Dialogue. My team and I met many scientists and specialist protected-area managers in China. We maintain excellent contact with the Chinese delegation, which has also visited Armenia's national parks," he said.
The success of COP17 will not end on Oct. 30, as Armenia will hold the COP presidency for another two years, he said.
He welcomed the Parties' strong willingness to advance work and their request for more time for negotiations. In the final stage of the conference, the presidency aims to produce a robust, objective global review. ■

articles.title: Russia Revives World War II-Era Arctic Shipping Route to Export Grain
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Russia Revives World War II-Era Arctic Shipping Route to Export Grain
Russia has begun using an Arctic maritime route dating back to World War II to export grain for the first time, Reuters reported on October 28. The move comes as Moscow seeks alternatives to traditional shipping corridors through the Black and Baltic Seas amid growing security risks stemming from its war against Ukraine.
To address these difficulties, Russia has been redirecting grain shipments from its southern agricultural regions to Baltic Sea ports, offering subsidies for rail transportation. At the same time, Moscow has begun exploring the Arctic as an alternative export corridor.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
On October 28, the Murmansk Commercial Seaport and Demetra Holding, one of Russia’s largest grain trading companies, announced that the first shipment of 3,400 metric tons of grain, transported from the country’s main agricultural regions, was being loaded onto a vessel at the port.
According to Reuters, the vessel is expected to carry approximately 28,000 metric tons of wheat from Murmansk to Casablanca, Morocco.
Located nearly 2,000 kilometers north of Moscow, near Russia’s border with Norway, Murmansk offers access to international waters. The port also has historical significance, having served as a major entry point for Allied supplies delivered to the Soviet Union during World War II.
“At a time when traditional export routes are facing restrictions, Murmansk Commercial Seaport is swiftly opening up an alternative route to foreign markets for Russian farmers,” the port said in a statement.
The development comes as Russia increasingly relies on Baltic Sea ports to maintain its grain exports.
According to Reuters, Russia exported approximately 1.2 million metric tons of grain through Baltic ports in September alone, accounting for more than 60% of its total seaborne grain shipments that month.
To accommodate the growing volumes, Russian companies have been converting port terminals previously used to handle fertilizers and coal into facilities capable of processing grain exports.
Russia has permitted grain-carrying vessels to leave the Sea of Azov for the first time since July, temporarily authorizing departures from the commercial ports of Temryuk and Kavkaz.
Citing three sources familiar with the situation, Bloomberg reported that the clearance was issued on October 26, with at least one vessel having already crossed the Kerch Strait into the Black Sea.
